channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: The Legend
item.description: Opens 'Saint Ned' by surveying a century of Ned Kelly worship, from Sidney Nolan's paintings and Arthur Boyd's sculpture to rival historians' verdicts, and argues Kelly's outlaw defiance of an entire police force answers a distinctly Australian craving for a hero who outwits authority.

item.title: The Making of a Paranoid
item.description: Traces Ned Kelly's Irish convict lineage through his father Red Kelly's transportation for pig stealing, his mother Ellen Quinn's family of horse thieves around Greta, and his own apprenticeship to the bushranger Harry Power, arguing his hatred of police was inherited before it was earned.

item.title: Massacre at Stringybark
item.description: Covers the Fitzpatrick incident that jailed Ned Kelly's mother and drove him into the bush, then the Stringybark Creek ambush in which Kelly and his gang shot dead Constables Lonigan and Scanlon and Sergeant Kennedy, turning him from horse thief into the most wanted outlaw in the colony.

item.title: Mr Kelly at Euroa
item.description: Follows the Kelly gang's first bank robbery, a genial, almost theatrical siege of Younghusband's Faithful's Creek Station and the Euroa branch of the National Bank in which Kelly charmed his hostages, dressed his gang in new clothes bought with stolen money, and rode off with £2060.

item.title: It's crunch time for Melbourne: we need a congestion tax
item.description: Argues Melbourne should follow London and Stockholm in adopting a congestion tax to break the city's addiction to the motor car, citing Bicycle Victoria figures on the rising share of peak-hour commuter cyclists.

item.title: Plagues be upon us, let's hope for no divine retribution
item.description: A mock-biblical catalogue of Melbourne's afflictions during a wet 2010, led by a possum population boom under the Wildlife Act, and running through cars, mobile phones, football and noisy restaurants via the ten plagues of Exodus.

item.title: Joy of sport lost in a country that takes it far too seriously
item.description: Reflects on Australia's outsized reaction to the 2010-11 Ashes loss under Ricky Ponting, arguing the country has forgotten that sport, unlike genuine disasters such as Cyclone Tracy, is meant to be enjoyed regardless of the result.

item.title: Swear fines a nonsense when invective is so ineffective
item.description: Marks new Victorian on-the-spot fines for swearing by recalling editor Michael Davie's landmark 1979 decision to print an obscenity in The Age, and proposes Paul Keating chair an inquiry into supplying Australians with fresh invective.

item.title: Once, footy dominated our lives. Now, things are much worse
item.description: Surveys the exponential growth of Australian Football League saturation since Keith Dunstan and Douglas Wilkie founded the Anti-Football League in 1967, from a single Saturday afternoon competition to year-round coverage, gambling and coaching sackings.

item.title: Oh, for the daily thud on my lawn
item.description: A tribute to the ritual of reading a printed daily newspaper in bed each morning, tracing Keith Dunstan's own newspaper family history against the decades-long death toll of Melbourne mastheads and Rupert Murdoch's prediction that print itself would be gone by 2020.

item.title: All I know about ethics, I learned at sword-point
item.description: Recalls a career of manufactured tabloid outrage, from a fake letters-page furore over Myer's window mannequins to a night spent hiding in a wardrobe from a sword-wielding husband, prompted by reflecting on the collapse of the News of the World.

item.title: Obituary: Walter Joseph Hauser
item.description: An obituary for Walter Hauser, one of the touring Vienna Mozart Boys' Choir singers stranded in Melbourne by the outbreak of war in 1939, who was taken in by Archbishop Daniel Mannix and went on to a career as an industrial chemist and Keith Dunstan's regular bridge partner.

item.title: Introduction
item.description: Explains that 'Sports' grew out of a 1969 La Trobe Library exhibition on Victoria's sporting past, and sets out Dunstan's aim to show that sport, not war or politics, is the true key to understanding the Australian character.

item.title: Our Sporting Obsession
item.description: Opens 'Sports' by arguing that sport is Australia's true national religion, tracing how politicians, Governors-General and even Prime Ministers have hitched themselves to football clubs and cricket teams to win public esteem, and how a colonial inferiority complex turned nineteenth-century sporting victories into proof the new nation could produce men and women equal to Britain.

item.title: A Bicycle Built for Two
item.description: The saga of acquiring, and riding, a proper touring tandem, from a doomed Malvern Star 'Cycle Master' that battered a Melbourne Cup wet-weather crossing to a hand-built Taylor Brothers tandem imported from a California bike shop after a customs battle lasting more than a year.

item.title: Bikecentennial '76
item.description: Dunstan, Marie and cartoonist Jeff Hook join 1200 riders pedalling the length of the United States for America's bicentenary, kitting out custom Sovereign Star bicycles with triple chainwheels under the guidance of gearing pioneer Ron Shepherd.

item.title: Oregon to Virginia
item.description: The Bikecentennial ride itself, 6750 kilometres from Reedsport to Yorktown through snowbound Rocky Mountain passes, tipi camps on Nez Perce country, dog attacks through the Ozarks, and a cyclone that finally stopped the Dunstans dunking their wheels in the Atlantic.

item.title: The Indefatigables
item.description: Chronicles the mania for covering distance on the high-wheeled bicycle, from century-a-day riders and George Burston and H.R. Stokes' 1888 circumnavigation to Arthur Richardson and Donald McKay's competing rides around Australia and Francis Birtles' seven crossings of the continent.

item.title: The Racing Wheel
item.description: A history of professional cycling's boom years at the Austral Wheel Race on the Melbourne Cricket Ground, dominated by the brilliant, scandal-prone American 'Plugger' Bill Martin and later by Major Taylor, before motoring killed the sport's popularity after 1906.

item.title: Oh, for a Malvern Star
item.description: Recalls the boyhood cult of the Malvern Star bicycle in Depression-era and wartime Melbourne, from Bruce Small's rise as its dealer and promoter of champion Hubert Opperman to Dunstan's own Sturmey Archer gears, speedometer obsession and boarding-house cycling at Geelong Grammar.

item.title: The Born-Again Biker
item.description: Traces Dunstan's own return to cycling during Melbourne's 1970s transport strikes, his time as founding president of the Victorian Bicycle Institute alongside Brian Dixon and Alan Parker, the campaigns for bike paths and the West Gate Bridge ban, and two mishaps that briefly cured him of the habit.

item.title: How to be a Nut
item.description: Opens 'The Confessions of a Bicycle Nut' by diagnosing "bike-itis" as a terminal, incurable virus, tracing Dunstan's own conversion from Bonnie Muir's fitness centre and 5BX exercises to jogging around East Malvern and finally to a lifetime on two wheels with his family.

item.title: The Love of the Wheel
item.description: Traces the bicycle's first golden age in Melbourne from the 1868 arrival of the velocipede through the reign of the high-wheeled 'ordinary' to the safety bicycle and pneumatic tyre, including the sad case of Bendigo rider W.J. Crowle, killed testing his 'Invincible' ordinary in 1884.

item.title: Biking in Bloomers
item.description: Recounts how women fought their way onto the 1890s bicycle craze against jeering larrikins, killjoy clergy and cumbersome skirts, from rational dress and Amelia Bloomer to the vice-regal enthusiasm of Lady Brassey and the illuminated cycle quadrilles staged by confectioner Macpherson Robertson.

item.title: Obituary: Richard Cudlipp
item.description: An obituary for advertising executive Dick Cudlipp, who rose to managing director of George Patterson Bates in 1965, drove Carlton and United Breweries' campaign against the Courage Brewery, and later became a Western District cattle and vineyard grazier.

item.title: A new clutch of ugly ducklings blots the cityscape
item.description: A nomination round for Melbourne's ugliest sights, from the Foxtel and Optus advertising signs looming over the historic Young and Jackson's Hotel to the kitsch interior of the new Imax Theatre and the warring columns of 101 Collins Street.

item.title: Harbor no grudge, it's better here; The bay and me
item.description: A Boxing Day case for Port Phillip Bay over its more celebrated rival, touring favourite spots from Sea Winds and Point Nepean to the Sorrento ferry and a flathead-fishing trip with mate Doug Crittenden.

item.title: Once a vision, now a site for sore eyes
item.description: The gutted, empty Southern Cross Hotel four years after the Nauru Government's redevelopment plans collapsed, and a look back at the lively Eastern Market it replaced in the 1960s, the market where C.J. Dennis's Sentimental Bloke first met Doreen.

item.title: Moombas and shakers
item.description: A profile of the Wittingslow family, the fairground dynasty who have run Moomba's rides and sideshows since patriarch Tom Wittingslow started out guessing weights at Penny Land in 1932, and who now stage the festival itself.

item.title: After 500 kilometres, still the kings (and queens) of the road
item.description: The 15th Great Victorian Bike Ride brings 2100 cyclists 500 kilometres from Wahgunyah to Melbourne, among them 83-year-old veteran Alan "Curly" Hartup and the ride's youngest finisher, nine-year-old Anna Clements.
